markdown.markdown: Instructor: Zahra Sadeghi # Lab ## Example 1 ### Create the Dataset ### Visualize the data We have a binary classification problem with two nonlinear classes. Our goal is to learn a decision boundary that separates them. 4. Create the K-Fold Cross-Validation strategy: "We divide the data into five folds. In each iteration, four folds are used for training and one fold is used for validation." ### Define a baseline MLP With solver="sgd", scikit-learn uses mini-batch gradient-based optimization by default. The default batch_size is "auto", which means: min(200, n_samples) ### Create a Pipeline The Pipeline ensures that preprocessing and model training happen together. During K-Fold Cross-Validation, the scaler is fitted only on the training portion of each fold, preventing data leakage." StandardScaler standardizes each input feature so that it has approximately: Mean = 0 Standard deviation = 1 z=(x−μ)/σ Create the train/test split Perform 5-Fold Cross-Validation This MLP works reasonably well. But are these hyperparameters optimal? ### Grid Search Grid Search with 5-Fold CV. GridSearchCV asks: "Which combination of hyperparameters gives me the best cross-validated F1 score?" | hidden_layer_sizes | Number of hidden layers | Heurons in each hidden layer | |:----|----:|:----| | (5,) | 1 | 5 | | (10,) | 1 | 10 | | (10, 10) | 2 | 10, 10 | | (20, 10) | 2 | 20, 10 | GridSearchCV already trained using best parameters Visualize the decision boundary ## Example 2 ### Generate the Dataset ### Visualize the Original Data ### Train MLP with Different Learning Rates ### Visualize Training Loss ### Visualize Decision Boundaries * Learning rate = 0.001: Updates may be small, leading to slower learning. * Learning rate = 0.01: May provide a good balance between speed and stability. * Learning rate = 0.1: Updates are larger, which may speed up learning or make it less stable. ## Example 3 ### Full-batch Gradient Descent One subtle point: in scikit-learn's implementation, the output activation is handled internally according to the classification task. activation="relu" only specifies the hidden layers. ### Stochastic Gradient Descent ### Mini-batch Gradient Descent ### Compare the Loss Curves ## Example 4 ### Create artificial moon data train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.15, stratify=y) Purpose: Preserves approximately the same proportion of each class in the training and test sets. For example, if your target variable contains 80% No and 20% Yes, both datasets will have approximately the same proportions. Use when: You are working on a classification problem, especially with imbalanced classes. groups = df['region'] stratify = groups #Preserves proportions of another categorical variable This approach is useful when you want to maintain the distribution of another categorical variable, such as region or demographic category. Now split the remaining 85% into training and validation. Entire dataset (100%) : x_tem (85%), x_test (15%) The class proportions should be approximately the same because of stratify. Class proportion = (Number of samples in the class) / (Total number of samples) ann.fit() — Training the model During training, the ANN: Takes the input features from X_train. Makes predictions. Compares its predictions with the actual labels in y_train. Calculates the error (loss). Adjusts its weights to reduce that error. Repeats this process over multiple training iterations. ann.predict() — Making predictions The purpose of predict() is to use the trained model to predict the target labels for the input data. X_test: The input features for the test dataset. y_pred: The labels predicted by the ANN. Unlike fit(), predict() does not train the model or adjust its weights. Macro F1-score measures a classification model's performance across all classes, giving each class equal importance regardless of how many samples it contains. ![Macro F1 Formula](img\macro-f1.png) K = number of classes. F1i = F1-score for class i. ![Weighted F1 Formula](img\weighted-f1.png) Weighted F1 calculates the F1-score for each class and weights it according to the number of actual samples in that class. K = number of classes. ni = number of actual samples in class i. F1i = F1-score for class i. cross-validation: Our validation set gives us one estimate of performance. But that estimate can depend somewhat on how we happened to split the data. 5-fold stratified cross-validation: Fold 1: TRAIN TRAIN TRAIN VALID Fold 2: TRAIN TRAIN VALID TRAIN Fold 3: TRAIN VALID TRAIN TRAIN Fold 4: VALID TRAIN TRAIN TRAIN Fold 5: TRAIN TRAIN TRAIN VALID
